questions.question: Q: Describe the agoge and its purpose.
questions.correctAnswer: The agoge was Sparta's state education system. Boys entered at age 7 and lived in communal barracks. They endured harsh physical training, were underfed to encourage resourcefulness, and were taught discipline, obedience and warfare. The purpose was to produce loyal, tough hoplites who would maintain Spartan military supremacy.

questions.question: Q: Why did the Spartans treat the helots so brutally?
questions.correctAnswer: Helots outnumbered Spartans by perhaps 7:1, creating constant fear of rebellion. The brutal treatment (random killings by the krypteia, annual declaration of war on helots) was deliberate state terror to prevent uprisings and maintain Spartan control of Messenia's agricultural land.

questions.question: Q: How was the Spartan government structured?
questions.correctAnswer: Two hereditary kings (from the Agiad and Eurypontid families) led the army and performed religious duties. Five ephors were elected annually and had powers to oversee kings, control education and try legal cases. The Gerousia (28 elders plus the kings) proposed laws. The apella (citizen assembly) voted on proposals but could not debate.

questions.question: Q: What was the krypteia?
questions.correctAnswer: A secret organisation of young Spartan men who patrolled the countryside at night, terrorising and killing helots. It served as both a method of controlling the helot population and as a final test in the agoge for prospective full citizens.

questions.question: Q: How did Spartan women differ from women in other Greek city-states?
questions.correctAnswer: Spartan women had significantly more freedom: they received physical training, could own and inherit property (since men were often at war), managed households independently, and were expected to produce strong children. They were famously told to come back from battle with their shield or on it.
